utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. As you can see, Judge Thelin is not able to sit this morning. Judge Van den Wyngaert and I will continue to sit under the rule. Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just a brief procedural matter. We actually like to request to the Trial Chamber to tender some documents from the back table next week. There are some documents which actually we have already seek leave to the Trial Chamber beginning of this week, which are the indictment and the judgement of the Belgrade Ovcara trial and there are just very few documents which have already been disclosed and some of the 65 ter documents, and we think we might run short of time this -- today, actually. So we would actually like to clarify this issue next week, if possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it the Defence has not had adequate time to be aware of these matters this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We actually put that into the e-court system but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then it would need, I would suggest, to be Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: That's fine with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a practical problem for anybody? Very well. It will be Monday afternoon, and we would sit at 2.15. I assume -- yes, we have a court available.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. No other matter then? The witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Could I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic. An hour 20 remaining, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we begin, I went through the transcript after the hearing and I saw that one word was omitted. We received an answer from the witness to a question. It had to do with berets. I asked whether it would be a blue, green, or a burgundy beret. At that time, berets were part of the uniform. So the word "burgundy" was omitted from the transcript, and we know why this is important. So there's no need to perhaps go through the tapes right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this would be sufficient, and the witness has already answered that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, yesterday, at the very end when I had already stopped talking you said that Radic was evidently present when the prisoners were beaten in front of the hospital. My question is: Would you be kind enough to provide some proof of that assertion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. You're actually misquoting me, because I didn't say that. I didn't say there was evidence that he was there when the prisoners were beaten; I said that there was evidence that he was in the hospital. Can I refer you, if you want an example, to four example. Witness P030, which is my footnote 126, where at line 973215 the witness said: "The officer occasionally addressed the person next to him, addressing him with: 'Captain Radic, carry out this search.'" He then goes on, referring to the activities of Major Sljivancanin, and he concludes at line 9734:2: "You've told us that he was giving orders and you used the name Captain Radic. Did you personally actually hear him use the phrase 'Captain Radic,' or is it something you've been told?" The witness answered: "He wasn't issuing orders to soldiers, but rather to the men standing next to him. He addressed him as 'Captain Radic.' He said that several times, four to five times, maybe even more, and I could hear it clearly." That is one example. If you wish to hear another --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We know what that witness told the Prosecution. My question is: When you were drafting the report, other than the statement of that one single witness, did you try to check through other witnesses who were together with witness P-030, information relating to the presence of Captain Radic, from witnesses who were captured, who were in front of the hospital, and who were searched? Did you find any trace in order to prove, without a reasonable doubt, a principle that applies to experts, to reach the conclusion that you reached in paragraph 75 [as interpreted] of your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can refer you to paragraph 84 of my report, I say: "It is apparent that Captain Miroslav Radic was" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise just for a second. There's a mistake in the transcript. It says paragraph 75 in the transcript, but the paragraph that I am referring to is paragraph 84. 84.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat, Mr. Borovic. There seem to have been a breakdown in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were working on your report, did you have access to evidence in relation to this point -- or rather, the presence of Captain Radic, as described by Witness 030? Any other witness who was together with Witness 030, they were all detained and they were next to this witness, and do any of these other witnesses describe this in a similar way and do you have any references to any such witnesses in the report that you drafted or was that the only statement that you used as proof of that particular assertion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, to begin with, that I looked at a whole host of documents which are annexed in my report. I didn't reference every single statement which appear -- which stated that Captain Radic was in the hospital, but I took -- I merely plucked out examples. In my original report, the example I actually quoted was see for exam -- see, for example - this is footnote 126 - Witness 61, Borivoje Tesic. Now, for reasons explained to the Court yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you just stop for a moment, please, General, sir. This is underlined in red. Yesterday I didn't want to interrupt you, so I allowed you to deal with that, but then now today again you're talking about Witness 61, Tesic. Actually, that witness did not testify before the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber doesn't know what you are talking about, although it would suit me very well for you to quote the entire statement by Tesic provided to the Prosecution, if you read it. And there are some other points, but I don't want to go into -- and follow that line of thought, although that would suit me very much. But are there any other testimonies, other than the testimony of Witness 030, and then we can finish with this topic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was simply answering your question. I'm sure there are. I haven't referenced them. I took example references just to state the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Since you cited only one example and not a number of them, then it would still be your position then that that was the only piece of evidence. My next question is --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not be my position. I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will leave that up to the Trial Chamber. Did you read what Witnesses Berghofer, Cakalic, (redacted), Karlovic, (redacted) stated in their testimony before this Trial Chamber? Did you read the statements of these witnesses given before this Trial Chamber or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Berghofer appears in my annex; Cakalic appears in my annex; (redacted) does not; Karlovic does; (redacted) does not. So it would appear I have read some of them but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are they in this group of 16 witnesses that -- whose statements you analysed or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have answered to the effect that those named by me are in my annex and they were, therefore, witness statements that I was given and I would have read them, the ones I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be redacted, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please give me a quote of any of these witnesses testifying to the fact that they were at the hospital on the 20th of November in front of the emergency entrance, and they were searched and boarded buses. Could you please quote any statement by any of these witnesses that would confirm what (redacted) said -- actually, I apologise, it's Witness P-030?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be a redaction as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If you don't, it's fine, we can continue so as not to lose any more time. I don't know if you referenced that in your footnotes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- the references in my footnotes are clear. I have not referenced the other statements and I consider it unreasonable to ask me to quote from their witness statements without having them on the screen so I can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir. You are defending your expert report and you should be prepared so that everything that you are charging the accused with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I'd suggest you get on with your cross-examination. The witness made it very clear he can't remember the detail of every statement he's looked at. If you want him to comment on a particular part, you need to put the statement to him. Otherwise, he has indicated generally what he relied on, but is not been able to remember the detail without refreshing his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I will do that. I didn't think that we could do it that way with the witness but it's reference 5279, line 21 of the transcript of March 1st, 2006. One of the witnesses stated the following: "When they searched us, I heard Major Sljivancanin saying that we had to board the buses. "Q. Who did he order this to? "A. To a person who looked as if he didn't have a rank. He was about 40 years old." Next question: "The situation in the barracks." The witness said on page 5459, line 6, to the question: "Do you recall anyone entering the buses and calling their names out," says: "No, I don't recall. Nobody read out any names. There were no lists, nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you read this statement by Witness Berghofer or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's in my annex, so if that's in his witness statement, I almost certainly would have read it, but it cuts against Witness P-030, who describes Captain Radic quite clearly calling out names at the buses at the JNA barracks, line 9739:20 of Witness P-030. "I saw no officers until the same Captain Radic from the hospital got on the bus carrying some kind of a list. Then he read out several names of the list, then these people got off the bus. That's the same Captain Radic from the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you stated this on a number of occasions, and we know about this, I just wanted to refresh your memory, Witness P031, transcript page 3240, line 4, of the 25th of January, 2006, stated in response to these same questions: "At that time, the JNA major was in charge of the whole operation. All of that was happening under his control and his orders." On page 3240, line 20: "Q. Did you see any other officer in a JNA uniform at that time, the 20th of November? "A. At that time, I didn't see any other JNA officer, but later I heard from prisoners who were together with me at the camp that there was another officer there in the hospital compound. He was a lieutenant and he participated in the searching of the people and escorted the people to the buses." On page 3248, line 4 to 20 he states in response to a question by my learned friend, the Prosecutor: "When you talked about the gentleman or the officer who entered the bus I think you used the word 'lieutenant.' Who was this lieutenant, did you see him before? "A. I don't know who that man was and I wasn't able to see him. He was standing at the front entrance of the bus, and that was the officer who was in charge of lining everyone up, physical searches, and escorting the prisoners to the buses." The Prosecutor asks: "May I try to clarify the situation so that there is no confusion or misunderstanding? You said that you encountered a major. Did you find out that that major or lieutenant was at the hospital? Now you're only talking about the lieutenant in the bus. The lieutenant whom you saw in the bus, is that the same lieutenant whom you saw at the hospital? "A. 'Yes.'" And so on and so forth. This is a second statement about that particular incident which does not correspond to the statement of Witness P-030. Did you review this statement, and as an expert who has to provide his expert opinion, check the differences in statements relating to the same event in order to reach your conclusion? Or did you think, because they don't confirm that statement, that that should not be referenced or given any importance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My expert opinion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt. My learned friend gave the pseudonym, but I think the witness himself does not know the name. And I obviously don't want that to be given in open court. But if the witness is to give a precise answer, it may well be advisable for the name to be given discreetly, either in written form or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moore, the witness was quite clear yesterday, and he quoted three names, the transcripts of whose testimony he used. He did not mention that particular name. So perhaps we don't need to mention the name and there would be no need for redactions. I'm going to finish that here. I'm just waiting for the response. I mentioned six names. I identified them, then we redacted some of them, and the question to the witness is whether anyone else confirms what Witness P-030 stated. I don't think the witness confirmed that, but I think we have lost a lot of time here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that on Croatian television for a long time the film titled --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I interrupt. You've asked me a question, you've gone on at length, you haven't allowed me to answer it. Can I comment on the question you asked me, and the lengthy transcript-selected sections that you have read out. There were no names in that. There is -- the transcript you read out talks about "a major." From my reading, I read that to be Major Sljivancanin, but he's not named. But I don't know. I'd have to see the whole statement. It also goes on at length about a lieutenant. Now, my immediate expert opinion question would be: Are you sure it's a lieutenant or could it have been a captain? How expert are you at telling the badges of rank? Because the only -- if it had said "captain," then it would have pointed immediately, in my expert opinion, because it ties up with P-030, to the captain being Radic. The fact that it is termed "a lieutenant" in the testimony, does not necessarily means it wasn't a captain. So I -- it doesn't prove that either he was there or he wasn't there, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, sir -- actually, the answer was not convincing in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not a matter, Mr. Borovic. I've many times had to comment to you about that, and our patience is getting short about it. It's not for you to offer your personal opinions to a witness. This witness will not be put off by them, but other witnesses can be and have been and it's very improper for counsel to do it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. But I do believe that the witness should be impartial in answering -- experts should be impartial when answering questions. Of course, I'm not obliged to respond to questions from the expert. But, Your Honour, I think that you are right. And I'm not going to abuse your trust, so it will just be question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you heard of the film "hundred days of Vukovar," which was shown throughout Croatia after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've heard it, but I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that in that film there is an officer, a captain, with moustache and a helmet, and who utters the following words: "Vukovar must fall tonight." And if I were to tell you that in the announcement preceding the TV showing of the film it was constantly said that this was Captain Radic, whereas in fact this is Captain Sasa Bojkovski, would you tell me whether you saw that particular excerpt from the movie where Sasa Bojkovski utters the words: "Vukovar must fall."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question. I said I haven't seen the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you this precisely because Witness P-030 stated here that he had seen this film and that he knew that a wrong name was linked with this person, that of Captain Radic. This was a propaganda carried out in the media, and this is something that the Prosecution ought to have checked. Witness P-002, do you know what this witness stated about whether he was present on the 20th of November in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not without you refreshing my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you read his statement -- or rather, transcript of his testimony here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appears as witness number 12 in my annex, so I think I probably read him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Witness 002 --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's referenced at footnote 12 -- my footnote 125, where I said: "Moreover he had his command post," that's Captain Radic, "collocated in the house of a local TO commander," and the witness statement for that is: "See, for example Witness" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, that's not what I'm referring to. General, sir, that's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about the hospital on the 20th of November. I asked you: Witness P-002 testified about that here in the courtroom. Have you read what he said to the Court and can you quote his statement concerning this fact? Do you know what Witness P-002 stated?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've seen Witness P-002's testimony, but please tell me what he did state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you should have seen this, but let me tell you what the witness said. First a video excerpt was shown to him. The witness confirmed that he was in that excerpt, which in turn confirmed his presence on the 20th of November in front of the hospital, as this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reference for Your Honours - it's a bit unusual for me to do this, but I see you are allowing it - 10494/18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry again. It depends exactly what my learned friend means by that question because I don't wish to pre-empt my learned friend, but my recollection is that that witness did not arrive until the actual -- what I will call the Ovcara evacuation, had left. And that was his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you spoke too soon, and I think it was improper of you to do that. We should have heard first what the witness had to say. I would like to kindly ask you not to suggest to a witness what she should give in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, were you following this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- may I say something? We've been quiet because we want to give you every opportunity to proceed the way you think best, but can I point out this. It's important, if you see the issue to be important, that you clarify with the witness whether -- which statements he has read of witnesses, which statements he specifically relied on, which testimonies he has read in addition to the pre-trial written statements, and which testimonies, if any, he's relied on. That's all important. But what is not important is to attempt, as it were, to put to this witness that there is evidence contrary from the evidence that he has actually relied on. You see, this expert has relied on certain factual matters and he's told you where he's got them from, a statement made by witness X, a statement made by witness Y, a book written by so-and-so, or whatever. Now, it's for this Chamber to weigh-up whether those sources are sufficient to establish the fact that the witness is proceeding to accept and to include in his expert opinion. It is for us to look at all the evidence, and in this case on any one fact there's bound to be a variety of evidence, some agreement, some disagreement, something of putting a different position altogether. And we have to weigh-up whether that is established or not. As long as we know what the witness has relied on, once we come to look at all the facts we can say: Was that proved or not? Were those witnesses reliable or not? And we can then conclude whether the witness was relying on what has proved to be reliable testimony or statements or something that we can no longer accept as reliable. Does that help you understand that you really don't need to go as far as you're going in this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I'm encouraged by what you said about what the Trial Chamber would do. I know that there would be a 98 Rule Conference, and I thought that I needed to clarify everything today. But all right, I have commenced with my question but I will not pursue it, except for wanting to wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This witness, whom I mentioned, who knows Captain Radic, said that he didn't see him there on the 20th of November in front of the hospital, nor did he see any other officer whom he could recognise there. So to conclude with this topic, as recommended by the Trial Chamber, if I were to tell you that there is a claim and that there is a witness who says: I'm the officer who conducted the frisking of the detainees and took them to the bus and I'm the officer who entered the bus with a list of 15 people, selected some of them, and then returned them to the hospital and, in a way, set them free, would that challenge your finding about the presence of Captain Miroslav Radic? And, my apologies, the witness also said: "I didn't see Captain Radic there."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not change my finding because my finding is based on witness statements that I have quoted. I note what you have said, and I assume there were more than one officer -- indeed, I know there were more than one officer at the hospital. It was a complex operation. There must have been a number of officers there and a lot of soldiers. So I don't see that the statement that you've read out, other than the statement that says he didn't -- he didn't see Captain Radic, maybe -- I can't comment on that or not. Maybe he was there, maybe he wasn't, maybe he was in a different part of the hospital when this particular witness was observing. I don't know. It doesn't change --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, it does not change my statement at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm overstepping my authorities, but the OTP has statements of these witnesses and I think that it should be a duty to ask to look at them following this. My next question: Can you tell us, very briefly, something about an attack at a populated settlement as a type of a combat activity? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighting in built-up areas, as I would describe it, is a dirty and messy business. It is extremely dangerous. It is a high-casualty, high-risk operation. It is difficult to command and control. Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. If that's all you have to tell me. My next question: When you spoke of resubordination, you explained that from the command and control aspect and you pointed out logistics as an important factor, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, that's correct. On your previous question, that's not all I had to tell you. I gave you the opportunity of whether you would wish me to go on or not. I take it you do not want me to go on. To the last question: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, thank you. Can you tell us how many levels down from the operations group can the detachments of Territorial Defence be resubordinated as well as detachments of volunteers in their entirety? Or in other words, if a commander of an operations group in his combat disposition has under his command the units that I mentioned, can such a commander resubordinate such units in their entirety to a commander of an assault detachment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's more properly a question for an expert on JNA doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you don't have the answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I couldn't be certain that the answer I gave you would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I will skip several questions. If I were to tell you that commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, Major Borivoje Tesic, toured the combat disposition only once, combat disposition of the 3rd Company where, except for Captain Radic, there was not a single officer because he lost all three platoon commanders, either to death or to illness, how would you then judge the responsibility of such a commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic's responsibility does not change because he has suffered casualties in his command --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My apologies. I meant commander of battalion. It wasn't recorded. It says just "commander" on the transcript. So how would you judge the responsibility of such a battalion commander? My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, I would assume that the battalion commander or assault detachment commander would raise that issue with Captain Radic, inquire as to whether his subordinate commands could still be effectively commanded by the next in the command chain, and if Captain Radic was content, that would be all right. But the commanding officer -- the detachment commander would realise there is some vulnerability in this command. If Captain Radic said no, he was in urgent need of reinforcements, if they were available, to help command his subordinate units or subunits, then there would be a responsibility, if it was possible to achieve, for the detachment commander to try and put that into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm receiving translation indicating that you said "detachment commander." Who are you speaking of if -- assuming that the interpretation is correct? I didn't ask you about any detachment commander.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the battalion -- yes, I used "detachment commander," perhaps instead of "battalion commander" because at this -- well, it depends on what stage you're talking about. But I think at some stage, yes, battalion commanders were the assault detachment commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, if that's what you meant. My follow-up question: Since I said that there were no other officers in that unit except for Captain Radic because he had lost all three platoon commander, he had three platoons, Tesic came only once. I asked you about how responsible that was of Tesic, not of Radic. And in relation to the command that you explained at length and that doctrine, was it a duty of a battalion commander to tour his subordinate commanders and units and to assess the climate and the situation? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say yes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can a company commander decide on his own to use TO detachments and Leva Supoderica Detachment in this same way as commander of Operations Group South or commander of an assault detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a company commander has had detachments such as you describe placed under his command, then he would have the responsibility for employing them in the manner that he thought fit --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I feel I'm getting the wrong interpretation. You say if a company commander has detachments under his command, a company commander cannot possibly have assault detachments under his command. Did you make a mistake or was it a case of wrong interpretation? Or are you claiming that a company commander can have assault detachments under his command? Would you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer your question at -- it's moving - line 49:18 when you said: "Can a company commander decide on his own to use TO detachments and Leva Supoderica Detachment in the same way as a commander of Operations Group South?" I said if he has detachments of TO, of whatever size, under his command, then he would use them in whatever way he thought fit. I'm not talking about assault detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can he, on his own, without authorisation of his battalion commander and commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, can the company detachment then decide on his own on using those units or is that decision up to the battalion commander or commander of the 1st Assault Detachment? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it depends on the organisation and the orders that the company commander has been given. If the company commander is, for example, effectively and -- please let me finish answering your question. If the company commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have very little time. My question is: Can he make such decision on his own without an order coming from his superior? So without such an order, can he decide on his own to use TO detachments and Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a company commander has been given TO troops under his command, he can use them as he likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And if no orders were issued, can he do it then? That was my question

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the TO troops have been placed under his command, it is up to him when and how to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If there is no order that they were placed under his command, what then? Can he still do it then?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect him to refer that to his commanding -- to his battalion commander because he would have a -- if he considered he had a requirement to use those TO troops and for the battalion commander to issue the appropriate instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a correct answer. General --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit 405, please, first? Could we pull that up in the screen in the English version so that the General can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order of the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade concerning blockade and attack, which was conveyed to the commanders within the Guards Motorised Brigade on the 1st of October, 1991. I'm going to read out to you the composition and tasks of the 1st Assault Detachment under the command of Major Tesic. I'm going to read paragraph 5. I already did that previously in this courtroom, but since you're an expert I would like to hear your comment. Paragraph 5 says: "1st Assault Detachment comprising 1st Motorised Battalion with the 3rd Platoon of the 1st Armoured Battalion, 2nd Platoon of the 2nd Company of light self-propelled artillery and rocket Battalion of the PVO, 1st to 3rd" -- I apologise, "the 1st Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion of military police and Pioneer Squad, commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Task: Bring up the infantry parts to the first sector to the achieved line during the night before first line on the 2nd of October, 1991, with guides from the Petrova Gora TO detachment. "Tanks and other equipment will be brought up during artillery preparations." And then another sentence: "In the beginning of the attack, in joint action with the 1st and 3rd Company of the TO, attack in the following sector ..." Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Can we agree that it is mentioned here that the 1st Assault Detachment is to act in joint action or in coordination as well as the TO detachment? This is the last sentence that I read. Are we -- can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "At the beginning of the attack, in cooperation with the 1st and 3rd TO," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. The commander of the Operations Group South, is he the person who has command over these tasks that I just read out, namely Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an order issued by OG South, commanded by Colonel Mrksic. The particular tasks you read out were to assault detachment I think number 1. Was it? You would have to scroll back up again. In which case, the tasks you've read out are the tasks to be carried out by assault detachment number 1 if that's the case. Could you scroll back up to the top of paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: "Tasks for the 1st Assault Detachment," yes, "but in coordination or joint action with Territorial Defence," which means that on that date on the 1st of October, they were all under the command of Colonel Mrksic at that point in time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that's correct, as Colonel Mrksic is giving this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. General, sir, please look at the screen. We will pull up Exhibit 408. This is a decision of the commander of the Operations Group South on the 15th of October, 1991. I will read out to you paragraph 2, which pertains to the 1st Assault Detachment. It says here: "1st assault attachment comprising 1st Motorised Battalion, 3rd Platoon of the 1st Company of the Armoured Battalion, 1st Platoon of the 2nd Company of the Military Police Battalion, and one volunteer company from the current combat disposition are to continue the attack in coordination with the 2nd Assault Detachment and 3rd/211 of the Armoured Brigade and Petrova Gora units," and so on. Is that what it says in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that at that point in time Colonel Mrksic, that is to say on the 15th of October, was the commander of these units and that he was issuing assignments to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at on the screen Exhibit 410, and this is a decision by the commander of Operations Group South of the 29th of October, 1991. I'm going to read item 2, paragraph 1, about the composition and the tasks of the 1st Assault Detachment under the command of Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Item 2, paragraph 1, it states: "The assault detachment one composition of the 1st Motorised Battalion, 1st Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the military police, detachment Leva Supoderica" --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I stop you. Can we get the right paragraph up on the screen. It's item 2, paragraph 1. That's item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Underneath there are assignments to units, this is under item 2, and then there is paragraph 1 of item 2. Do you have it on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we've got it. Unit tasks: 1st Assault Detachment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The assault detachment 1 comprising: "1st Motorised Battalion, 1st Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Battalion of the military the Leva Supoderica detachment, the Petrova Gora detachment, volunteers company of Novi Sad, and one M-84 tank," and so on and so forth, is tasked with the assignment that you see on the monitor. Did I read that out correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that the commander -- now that we're talking about Assault Detachment 1, whose composition I've read out to you is Major Borivoje Tesic, that he is now, for the first time, taking over these powers from Colonel Mrksic in the sense of direct command. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment has got these units that you've read out in paragraph 1 under his command. I -- if that's what you're saying, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we look at Exhibit 430 on the screen. It's a decision by the commander of OG South of the 14th of November, 1991. Can we now look at item 2, assignments to the units, and I'm going to read paragraphs 4 and 5 under that heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 of paragraph 2: Tasks to the units, it says: "Assault Detachment 1 (minus the 1st Motorised Battalion) from the current region of combat disposition transferred to be the Dalmatinska-Alijagica and water-tower sector." Is that what it says in item 2, paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it -- should it read minus or is that assault detachment 1 1st Motorised Battalion. Or does it mean minus the 1st Motorised Battalion which is what it says? I'm not sure, but I agree with what you've read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. In the original order it says "minus the 1st Motorised Battalion." You read it correctly. Now I'm going to read out to you item 5. "1st Motorised Battalion from the present region of combat disposition, secure the reached line, establish full control over the captured area, and engage in coordinated action with the attacking forces along the Sundarciceva Street and Marsala Tita Street. Be on stand-by for active combat along the Milovo Brdo bridge's axis." General, can we agree that Major Borivoje Tesic, to whom OG South commander assigned this task at the point in time when Assault Detachment 1 -- or actually, transferred the 1st Motorised Battalion of the 1st Assault Detachment to a different axis, which I read to you from paragraph 5, can we agree that Borivoje Tesic is still the commander of the Assault Detachment 1 and at the same time is responsible for his own basic unit, the 1st Motorised Battalion, regardless of the fact that they were in two different sectors or along two different axes of operation? Is he responsible, both for the 1st Assault Detachment and for the 1st Motorised Battalion, even though they were on different axes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me from what we've seen in this order on the screen so far what the remainder of the 1st Assault Detachment is tasked with. You've shown me what 1st Motorised Battalion is tasked with and then there's 2nd Motorised Battalion. I'm not quite sure -- is there a task for Assault Detachment 1 remnants? We'd have to screen on -- we'd have to roll-on --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, paragraph 4 is important. This is why I read both 4 and 5 to you. In paragraph 4: "The main strength of Assault Detachment 1 without the 1st Motorised Battalion is being transferred from the current area of combat disposition to the Dalmatinska Street, Alijagiceva Street, and the water-tower axis." And the 1st Motorised Battalion is on this other access, which I read out to you from the water-tower access. Is that in order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in order. I'm starting to feel sorry for Major Tesic because he is not only -- as I understand it, he is not only the commander of the -- he's the commander of the all-arms mix of the assault detachment. There seem to be two different taskings here. When it says the assault detachment relocate to the -- if that's just a move of location rather than an attacking task, maybe he can put his assault detachment remainder to one side and get on with commanding his 1st Motorised Battalion in his combat operation on that axis, but I haven't got the whole order in front of me. But it would appear that he is commanding the assault detachment and his motorised battalion at the same time doing different tasks; quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you are right. It is not easy to answer. Can we look at Exhibit 431. Sir, this is a decision by OG South commander dated the 16th. This is two days later, the 16th of November, 1991. I'm going to read paragraph 1, and then in paragraph 1, item 2. Do you have that on your screen? There is also item 1. You can see that. It's not so important for my question where it says: "I hereby decide." What is important for my question is: "Task it is to the units: 1." "1st Motorised Battalion in line with the task of 14th November, 1991," and that is actually item 5, General, from the decision of the 14th of November, 1991, "with support of part of the forces of the armoured battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade continue the attack on the Sundarciceva Street - Rade Koncara estate bridges over the Vuka river and by 1600 hours on 17 November seize the area surrounding the bridges over the Vuka river, Marsal Tito Street. From which location. Be ready to continue the attack over the Trg Republike towards the Danube, Marsal Tito Street and Stjepana Radica Street." My question for you is: What is this fact in accordance with -- or in line with the task of the 14th of November, 1991, mean? Is it correct what I submitted to you that the 1st Motorised Battalion should act in line with the task of the 14th of November, 1991, from paragraph 5 which I read to you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Reinforced further by elements of the armoured battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please now tell us, according to your best knowledge, and I think that you make quick analysis. On the 16th of November, under whose control were the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica TO detachments?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that order put them under control of the 1st Assault Detachment, did it not? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You are quite correct. And now my question: Did you have access, as an expert, to any documents in the course of your analysis, any decision or command at the OG South operational command after the 16th of November which significantly changed the situation in terms of responsibility over the TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica detachments until the combat operations were over or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one that immediately comes to mind is the resubordination order of I think the -- I think it was the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thinking of the 21st, this is why I'm asking the question. During the combat operations, this is where we stop, and then about the rest we already know about that. The combat operations were until the 18th of November, 1991. Did you come across any such documents or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have done. The orders, 1st Military District OG South documents are at paragraph 2 of my annex. If there are any in there that you're referring to, I will have seen them. But if you want me to be specific, please put up on the screen what you want me to specifically comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And specifically, these things that I asked you about, there is no document on any of that but I wanted to be absolutely thorough and I wanted to be sure that perhaps you didn't have access to any document that I didn't really come across. So I don't have anything to put on the monitor and I'm sure you might have something more to say. Well, all I have is five minutes, so perhaps we can proceed quickly. Very well. Quoting paragraph 25 of your report as confirmation of your assertion that there were assault detachments, you cited the testimony of Witness Trifunovic and Witness P-022. Witness Trifunovic mostly speaks theoretically about the assault groups and I'm not going to go into these theoretical remarks because that testimony from the standpoint of Mr. Radic's Defence was quite correct and we're not going to go into any other things. What I'm interested in is the following: Based on the testimony of Witness P-022 and citing that witness in your footnote you confirmed the existence of assault groups. You did not read a statement by a witness who appeared in this trial, before this Trial Chamber, and the reference for the Tribunal is transcript page 5077, line 20, where this witness you, because it is only one example --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, should I present this excerpt to the witness or should we just leave it at the reference for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When he talks about the assault detachments and the joining of the volunteers and the TO to the companies, you discussed that and you relied on the testimony of Witness P-022.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg the Court's indulgence. I just need a little bit more time. I just have two or three more questions, so I would like to ask the witness to respond this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So page 5077, line 20, I asked the Witness: "What does the word 'incorporate' mean?" And the witness said: "No." He didn't know. The question is: "Is this the first time you heard this word being used?" The witness said: "Yes. The lawyer's question: "The Prosecutor investigator asked you whether Territorial Defence people were incorporated into Captain Radic's unit and your answer was yes. How could you affirmatively answered that question if you did not know what the word 'incorporate' means or was that not your answer?" The witness said: "I said we were together." "This is a different question. My question was specific." Witness answers: "I told you what I meant then when I said that. That's what I said."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: "Does that mean that they were not incorporated in Miroslav Radic's company, the people from the TO?"

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They were together, i.e. we were together, the people of the Territorial Defence, the volunteers, we were all together on the same axis," and I underline this, General, "as well as the 3rd Company. "Do we agree that they were together only for as long as the combat operations lasted on the same axis?" Witness responded: "Yes." General, sir, based on what I have just read out to you, can we agree and can you conclude that the witness asserts that the TO and the volunteers were not incorporated into the 3rd Company, but they were together in -- during the combat operations, along the combat axis only during the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make an initial comment because you've put up various tasks to the assault detachments, and you've laid out in these orders what the assault detachments consisted of. These are sizeable organisations that cannot be commanded as an entity. They would have to be subdivided into subunits in accordance with the assault detachment commander's wishes. And therefore, I would expect those subunits to be a mixture of whatever all-arms groupings he wanted, infantry, armour, engineers, TO, volunteers, in accordance with his orders. Therefore, it doesn't come as any surprise to me that the 3rd Company is operating together with TO under its command to achieve a specific objective. Now, you -- in my opinion, you could call that an assault group, and indeed Witness P-022 describes Captain Radic as commanding TO or volunteers in exactly that way. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have absolutely given the wrong answer because what I have read out does not say anywhere that Miroslav Radic was the commander of that group. What it says is that Territorial Defence was not incorporated into his 3rd Company and that they just were along the same axis of operations. I was very specific. All the more because the Territorial Defence has its own commander. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says: We were all together on the same axis. My immediate question would be: Under whose command?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Axis of operation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. If we're all together on the same axis, unity of command, that command and control principle, they must have been under someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There's a commander of the 3rd Company, and there's a commander of the Territorial Defence. The position of the Defence of Miroslav Radic was that they were not under the command but in coordinated action, and this is already in the evidence that we have presented so far. I have ten seconds left. You quoted Witness P-022 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 002, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that this witness said that Miroslav Radic found out what happened at Ovcara because the witness, P-002, spoke with the TO commander about the crime at Ovcara, and that this was sufficient information for him to know and not to have done anything. I'm talking of Miroslav Radic. Since you say you did not review the transcript of the testimony of the Witness P-002 in this trial, we reviewed a number of incidents relating to this witness and we never found any instance of him talking with the commander of the Vukovar TO in the presence of Miroslav Radic. He even said that he asked what happened, that he had just waved his hand and said: Excuse me, it's a bloody mess. But he never said that he spoke with Radic on that evening and not in the morning when he was together with the TO commander. And in some places he even said that this happened a few days later. I am finished, so I am presenting this to you and I am telling you of the position of the Defence of my client, as this is a requirement on the part of the Prosecution. There is no order after the 14th of November, 1991, from which it could be seen that the Territorial Defence and the Leva Supoderica detachments were in any kind of contact or even in the combat disposition with the company of Captain Miroslav Radic. I'm also asserting to you that after the 18th of November, the assault detachment of one -- Assault Detachment 1, the TO volunteers, and the Leva Supoderica detachment were no longer even under the command of Borivoje Tesic, under whose command they were, you know in which period. But as of the 18th of November they were no longer under his command, and this is something you can find in the statement of his you read, provided to [as interpreted] the Prosecution, where he clearly talks about the oral order of General Mrksic of the 18th of -- as of the 18th of November, the TO and the Leva Supoderica detachments were no longer under his command. He did not take part in any kind of evacuations of the hospital on the 20th of November, 1991, and Miroslav Radic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This apparently is supposed to be a question. I see it has "Q" at the start at 32:2. My learned friend has attempted to make a statement to try and get into evidence material that he knows the Prosecution do not rely upon for very good reason. If my learned friend has a question, he can put the question, but he shouldn't make the statement for his own purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the statement has been made, Mr. Moore. We've allowed Mr. Borovic to do so. It's one upon which the witness can hardly comment, given the variety and length of subject matter, and it's one upon which it has no force other than that of submission. Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And thank you for allowing me to exceed my time a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll now have the morning break, and because of the redaction we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm the last of the last. I'm the last Defence counsel to examine the last witness here. General Pringle, I'm Novak Lukic. I'm Defence counsel of Veselin Sljivancanin. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of his team. Let's clarify this to see if it's a technical error. On page 12 it says that you retired in 1991, page 12 of your report, and yesterday you said to Mr. Moore that you retired in 2001. So can we clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday Mr. Moore corrected that. That is a typing error. It should read "2001."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your biography I found certain references that I think will be very useful in relation to the topics that I'm interested in. I see that you worked at high-level posts, including counter-intelligence duties. And I think that you will be especially competent to clarify this portion of your report. First of all, let's look at some of the aspects of command and control. I already have some linguistic complaints to make, but I will leave that for later. There are many definitions of the command and control concept. I went over a lot of documents that were introduced into evidence here, but except for the common definition of command and control as a doctrine, I didn't find a separate definition for the control portion. And I see that you did define that in your report. Command and control are certainly not the same notion, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer that, can I just correct a statement you've made. I have never worked in counter-intelligence duties. To answer your question, command and control are intricately linked together, but they are not the same notion. Command encompasses the authority and responsibility and duty to act. Control is much more about the coordination of activities required, usually by the staff, in order that -- in order to facilitate the execution of the commander's orders or commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We seem to be on the similar wavelength. You defined that in article 16 of your report, where you said that control is a means through which a commander implements orders. But would you agree with me that it's not exactly a means but a process aimed at preparing the unit, making a decision, and later on implementing this decision. I see control as an activity, active implementation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. I can see you've read my report where I say: "Control is the process through which a commander, assisted by his staff, organises, directs, and coordinates the activities of the forces allocated to him," paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 34, 24, there is an error. You'll see it only relates to encompasses. That should also have command in front of it. It hasn't been altered, but it better be altered now because it is important. There --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see the line reference, unfortunately, is always different from yours. I've found the reference now. 34, 24, it actually did have a word there that was incorrect, and I suspect the stenographer has removed it. But it should read, "Command encompasses the authority" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and responsibility and duty to act, which is what I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the witness said and is what Mr. Lukic also understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. This clearly stems from the report of the witness and how he understands the doctrine of command and control. Would you please take tab 96 bis, please, General. I think that you have -- or rather, this tab related to your footnote 96 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're interested in Exhibit 107. I think we all have the tabs in front of us. No need to pull them up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at article 7, 7 (d). Based on the terminology of security organs, I'm clarifying this because the term "control" in B/C/S language is used in the command and control doctrine, but there is also the term called control in the technical, professional sense, especially since where it is used for military police purposes. If you look at 7 (d), you will see that it says there that: "The security organ participates in specialist control of military" I'm quite happy with this English translation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the page number of that? That's not what it says in my 7 (d).

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The very beginning. I will give you the English version. Page 8, it begins on page 7 and then goes on on page 8. It's subparagraph (d). [In English] "Performing special administration services for military police unit."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw in the annex that you also studied the rules of service of the military police. It's not included in the reference, and maybe you'll remember it. And do you remember that there is this same definition in that document when regulating the relations between the military police and the security organ?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did study the rules of service of the military police. Unfortunately, I haven't got them in the tabs. 7 (d) is taken from the rules of service of the security organs, and from reading those documents I'm aware of a fairly intimate relationship - shall we put it like that - between the security organs and the military police, with the security organs tasked with specific responsibilities for, in particular, training and advice and employment of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this is a special section in your report, we will get to that. I'm now interested in the command and control aspect, and later on we will get to the special nature of that relation. I studied the textbook for military academies for 1983 where there is a definition of command that seems quite interesting to me. I will thus ask you whether you will agree with my definition that the command includes the decision-making right and right to assign tasks?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. And indeed at paragraph 16 of my report I say: "Thus leadership and decision-making are his" -- where I'm talking about a commander, "are his primary responsibilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The doctrine of singleness of command is something that you discussed, as did Mr. Theunens. That means that there is just one superior officer in command. You said that yesterday on page 15, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what unity of command describes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the subordinate is responsible only to him, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subordinate is responsible to his immediate commander, but he also carries responsibilities for those he commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. I wasn't going to debate the notion of responsibility -- rather, the links. So this control, be it in the specialist terms or the one concerning the security organs, does not also include decision-making and task assigning, correct? In your report you said that the security organ is subordinated only to his commander. So I'm asking you now: Under your definition of command, the principle of singleness of command and subordination, the control in the specialist sense doesn't include any of these other aspects of command that I just asked you about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rules for security organs describe all these functions. Would agree entirely that the security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer, command unit, institution or staff of the armed forces and whose strength it is placed in the establishment, see paragraph 16, chapter 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please look at article 18; it has to do with my next question. The security organ of the superior establishment command, can it and is it authorised to issue an order to security organ from a lower establishment unit or can it only give some specialist guidance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here you enter into an interesting command and control arena or one that I found particularly interesting in exploring the functions of security organs. It is quite clear that a security organ is responsible to the commander in whose formation it sits, but it is also quite clear to me that there is a web of links amongst security organs, both upwards, downwards, and sideways, in addition to that. Now, that does not, in my reading of this, assume that a superior security organ has the right to give orders to a subordinate -- or to a security organ in a subordinate formation. It does, as paragraph 18 describes, provide specialist administrative services for security organs in subordinate commands. And I've come to that conclusion because JNA doctrine is very firm on unity of command. And you would end up with confusion if the security organs were taking orders from their immediate superior commander and down some parallel security organ chain. So I don't think that is what happens. But there is a security organ cobweb of information that is flowing in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm quite satisfied with this answer. I fully agree with you. I'm going to ask you something that you put in your report under the command and control principle in OG South. You received documents from the Prosecution, and you spoke of that from paragraph 22 onwards in your report. I'll ask you this: Did you see any documents -- were there any documents which you used as a source to write about the relations between security organs and OG South? Simply speaking, did you see any document which would lead you to conclude about the relations between security organs of OG South and OG South?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My primary sources of research on security organs were the rules for security organs and also the rules for military police, from which I drew deductions about the command and control relationship and the sort of relationship that the head of a security organ would have with his immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, although we already heard this answer, though I will repeat it through a line of my questions. Within an operations group, each unit has its own area of responsibility, which is clearly defined through the orders of the operations group commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we heard the position of the Prosecution, namely that on the 20th of November, 1991, Ovcara was within the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ovcara was within the zone of responsibility of OG South, and in subdividing that zone of responsibility the commander had delineated particular areas to subordinate formations. And Ovcara lay in that subdivided area of responsibility that was the responsibility, I believe you're correct, of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said to Mr. Vasic, and we were able to see that based on the annex, that when writing your report you did not have available to you a single document on the 80th Motorised Brigade. I'm asking you this: As you were writing your report and when you read statements of Vojnovic and Vezmarovic, did you ask the Prosecution whether they had any document of that unit? In other words, in your research did you ask for certain documents to be provided to you by the Prosecution, if they had them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents I was using for my research were provided by the Office of the Prosecution. I didn't ask for extra documents. I didn't what documents existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you will agree with me that yesterday when you saw the log-book of the 80th Brigade and all the facts stated therein, you concluded that that would have been useful for you, helpful for your report. But I'll ask you this: Based on the statements that you used pertaining to the 80th motorised brigade and based on the documentation of the Operations Group South that you used, can we conclude that the 80th Motorised Brigade and its commander, that commander, Vojnovic, had command and control over that brigade pursuant to all principles in force in the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a statement of the obvious that the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade had full command and control over the 80th Motorised Brigade. If that's what you're saying, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely that. Precisely that. Naturally, this brigade carried out the assignments given to it by the commander of OG South.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is that a question or a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You could take it as both. I suppose you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were making a statement. I -- either way I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we rely too much on leading questions and the form prescribed. In paragraph 35 of your finding you said that what happened in the end was almost fully foreseeable in view of the brutal conduct of TO units and given the well-documented ill discipline of them. I'll say this: Based on the questions that were put to you yesterday, I took it that you, in your report, after studying documentation and witness statements, did not conclude that on the 18th of November, in Mitnica, which is a suburb of Vukovar, there were negotiations held and then a large number of Croatian defenders, if I may call them that, soldiers, surrendered to the JNA. After spending one day -- or rather, one night at Ovcara, all of them to the last one, I think that 187 of them were transferred to a prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Did you know this fact when writing your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm generally aware that some successful and well-conducted evacuation operations had been executed before the 20th of November, but I remind you again, my report is based on answering some very specific questions. But I agree, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is how I, as a layman, am thinking. Do you fully uphold your finding, this conclusion -- or rather, would it change your conclusion had you known that just two days prior to that there was an activity related to surrender, escort, and further escort of detained persons, and that all of this was carried out successfully in that same area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's precisely of that that I find it so surprising what happened on the 20th of November. What happened on the 20th of November was conducted in a different way, I believe by different people, apparently in a very much more confused command and control situation. And perhaps that is why -- perhaps that contributed to what happened. But the fact that there was some successful evacuation operations on the 18th does not mean that -- well, it makes it more surprising that the operation on the 20th was conducted in the rather shambolic way that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree here with what you used, "surprising"; that's the term you used in your answer. But in your report you used the word that it was predictable. So these are two completely different terms. Let me just check the term that you used in English.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm happy to take that as a question. I'm talking about in paragraph 35 the events of the 20th of November. The events of the 20th of November, in my view, were entirely predictable by an experienced commander who knew that the evacuation of the hospital comprising a mixture of combatants, noncombatants, women, children, wounded, non-wounded, a very complex event, would have had to have been very carefully controlled and specific orders given. And in particular any involvement of TO forces and irregulars would immediately spark warning signs in an experienced commander's mind. The fact that those people were used as part of that operation I think means, in my opinion that what happened was predictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. Let us not spend too much time on this topic. Let us just clarify one thing. I will skip over something, but it is in the same context. In paragraph 74 of your report you say that the members of local TO may assist in identification of residents and that they could be helpful for security organs in the process of triage. This is what we call as triage. Based on this conclusion I would like to ask you this: Did you find any other document or any other statement indicating that the TO members acted differently in the hospital itself on the 20th of November, so the day of evacuation? We know that all of this was taking place between 7.00 a.m. and 10.30 a.m., so within that time-frame. Did you find any evidence that the TO members acted in a different manner, acted differently than what you wrote in paragraph 74?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If I recall correctly, there were witness statements to the effect that TO and/or irregulars were behaving in a brutal manner towards prisoners. I believe there was a statement to the effect that a number of prisoners were being kept in a cell who were apparently badly beaten up, and they were denying access to regular JNA officers. So I think there's plenty of witness statements to the effect that the TO/irregular troops were acting in an ill disciplined way. And I quote from my report: "Given their reputation for ill discipline and a consequent very ill risk of revenge," they would have to be very controlled and organised. They would have their uses, particularly in terms of identifying people, because they were local troops. But any experienced commander would realise that that also carried with it dangers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't understand each other and perhaps we did and that was your answer. What you mentioned about the testimony, I link that to the previous evening. I asked you about a specific time period. That is the moment of evacuation, as it is termed by the Prosecution in the indictment, meaning taking out the persons who happened to be at the hospital after triage -- well, we don't have to use that term. But anyway, taking out the persons and then later taking the same people to the barracks or Ovcara. Do you have a statement by any witnesses for that period that members of the TO behaved differently from the way you described in paragraph 74? And if you do, could you please give us an example?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me one moment. I don't think I have a statement to hand to that effect, but my recollection from the thousands and thousands of pages of witnesses' testimony that I have looked at and scanned was that there was indeed evidence -- or statements, not evidence, statements to the effect that the TO and irregular troops were acting in a brutal manner. But I'm unable to lay my -- to point to a specific witness statement straight from the top of my memory I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried in formulating this question - and I do understand that the materials were vast in quantities, but I did want to have a clear position on this. I, other than what you mentioned in paragraph 74, did not find that they were behaving brutally and in an undisciplined way in the hospital or the hospital courtyard at that time. And I did not find that there were volunteer units there at that point in time. But very well, you gave me the answer that you have given at this point, and we can continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a question with a very -- you asked me a question with a very specific time-frame, a bracket of two hours I think you gave me. I can't -- generally in the hospital I have read statements to the effect that the TO and irregulars were there acting in a brutal manner. Whether that was in that two-hour time-frame, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what you assert in your conclusion -- actually, in your findings it relates to the general conduct and general events in the hospital. It does not only encompass that very brief time period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
